questions.q: What does a high volume of SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD indicate?
options: Tasks are repeatedly yielding the CPU after their scheduler quantum because other runnable tasks are waiting for that scheduler — a strong signal of CPU pressure
The transaction log is full
A query is blocked waiting on a row lock
The buffer pool is undersized
questions.explain: SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD is recorded specifically when a task's time slice ends and other runnable tasks need that scheduler, directly reflecting CPU/scheduler contention.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is a high total wait time on CXPACKET automatically a problem?
options: No — it's a normal part of parallel thread synchronization; it's worth investigating mainly when paired with thread skew or unnecessary parallelism on small queries
Yes — any CXPACKET wait means parallelism must be disabled instance-wide
No — CXPACKET only ever appears due to a hardware failure
Yes — CXPACKET always means MAXDOP is set incorrectly
questions.explain: High CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER time reflects that the instance runs a lot of parallel plans, which can be entirely appropriate; the actual concern is skew or inappropriate parallelism, not the wait type's presence alone.

questions.q: Which DMV, and which column, identifies the queries actually consuming the most CPU time?
options: sys.dm_exec_query_stats, ordered by total_worker_time
sys.dm_os_wait_stats, ordered by wait_time_ms
sys.dm_exec_requests, ordered by session_id
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats, ordered by num_of_reads
questions.explain: total_worker_time in sys.dm_exec_query_stats is cumulative CPU time in microseconds since the plan entered cache — the direct measure of CPU consumption per query.

questions.q: Why is sorting by total_worker_time better than sorting by total duration when hunting for CPU-heavy queries?
options: Duration can be dominated by time spent waiting on something else, not actually working the CPU, so it can mislead you about what's truly CPU-expensive
Duration and total_worker_time are always numerically identical
total_worker_time is measured in a different, incompatible unit that can't be compared across queries
Sorting by duration is actually the better choice in every case
questions.explain: A query can have a long duration mostly from waiting (I/O, locks) rather than CPU work; total_worker_time isolates the CPU-time component specifically.

questions.q: sys.dm_os_wait_stats shows CXPACKET as a top wait type by total time, but every parallel query's actual execution plan shows evenly balanced row counts across threads. What should you conclude?
options: This is likely normal parallel-execution overhead, not a problem worth chasing, since there's no thread skew present
This definitively proves a CPU bottleneck that must be fixed immediately
The wait stats DMV must be reporting corrupted data
Parallelism should be disabled instance-wide as a precaution
questions.explain: Without skew or evidence of inappropriate parallelism on small queries, high CXPACKET time reflects expected synchronization overhead from legitimately parallel plans.
